scope: Assigned nonempty-choice boundary rows only; one targeted Statement/Definition and proof read per item.
normalizer_review: Read tools/boundary-audit.mjs: quoted and mathematical spans are removed in clustering; rows therefore record distinct actual choice operations and hypotheses in unquoted prose. No template_review exemption used.

rows.reasoning: Dependent Choice is assumed in the Statement and Given. In step 1.1 a single compact-time operator bound M comes from F1, whose uniform boundedness argument uses DC; steps 1.2 and 1.3 then fix one vector and estimate its right and left increments. They select neither a family of vectors nor witnesses for all times simultaneously.

The DC assumption supplies the finite supremum M0 in F1 through local boundedness. Step 1.1 separates the zero space, where M=1 and omega=0 are explicit; otherwise M is that supremum and omega its uniquely defined logarithm. Step 2.1 uses the deterministic floor decomposition of each time. No choice of norm-attaining vectors is used.

For a fixed x in D(A), steps 1.1 and 2.1 transport the already existing generator quotient limit through the fixed bounded T(t). The only choice-sensitive input to step 3.1 is the compact-time bound in F3, covered by the declared DC assumption. The left derivative estimate uses this bound and orbit continuity, without selecting vectors indexed by h.

DC is explicit and its Countable Choice consequence is used in step 3.1 to infer graph closedness from the convergent-graph-sequence criterion. Density in step 1.1 uses the explicitly defined averages t^{-1}J_t x for each x; it does not select approximating points from arbitrary dense sets. The closedness estimate uses the local bound in F3, also under DC.

Step 4.1 explicitly chooses a sequence y_n in the dense domain converging to the fixed y. This is a countable selection, licensed by the Statement assumption DC. The other approximants J_R are specified integrals, and graph integration in step 1.2 uses finite partition samples. The declared DC also covers the closed-generator and local-bound suppliers; no arbitrary-index selection is required.

In step 1.1 one real lambda0 between omega and lambda is fixed to dominate nearby difference quotients; for example their midpoint works. Steps 2.1 and 4.1 use tail estimates and induction rather than selected norm maximisers or infinitely many independent representatives. DC is expressly assumed and covers the Laplace and Bochner inputs; the positive integer m gives a finite induction stage for each formula.

DC is available throughout the Yosida construction. For each fixed x and error tolerance, step 3.1 uses one y in the dense domain and then its Cauchy estimate; the limit T(t)x is uniquely determined, so the proof does not select among multiple possible limits for all x. The approximants A_lambda are fixed resolvent expressions, and the compact-time majorant in step 1.1 is explicit.

The Statement assumes DC before either direction. Sufficiency in step 1.1 consumes the Yosida construction with exactly that principle; necessity in steps 1.2 and 1.3 consumes the closed-generator, Laplace, and power-estimate results under DC. The resolvents and the constructed semigroup are determined by these arguments, rather than selected from an arbitrary family of generators.

DC is the stated hypothesis for the specialised Hille-Yosida input F1. The reverse implication in step 1.2 obtains every power estimate by finite multiplication of the single resolvent bound; no additional sequence of witnesses is chosen. For the complex extension in step 2.1, density and closed-graph integration use the same DC-backed Laplace argument, with a uniquely defined J_z.

After a single positive surjectivity parameter lambda0 is given, step 2.1 propagates the resolvent using the explicitly prescribed lambda_k=(3/2)^k lambda0. The inverse at each parameter is unique by dissipativity. In step 3.2 the y solving (lambda I-A)y=(lambda I-A′)x is likewise unique, so this pointwise argument adds no choice principle. DC remains explicit for the contraction-generation supplier.

The choice uses are identified in Given: DC covers the closed graph theorem applied to Phi in step 2.1, and Countable Choice covers the contradiction witnesses (x_n,t_n) in step 1.3 and the sequence approximating a fixed x in D(B) by D(A). Step 4.2 selects one term of an already given unbounded lambda_n sequence, which requires no independent choice. Thus the declared DC covers the actual selections.

DC supplies the local bound and closed-generator inputs used in steps 1.3 and 3.1. The simple f_n in step 1.3 are defining Bochner approximants; their graph integrals are obtained from finite partition samples, and the approximation of g in step 2.1 is within the same framework. Integral-solution uniqueness in step 1.4 uses a vanishing derivative, without selecting solutions for a family of data.

This lemma assumes both DC and HB in the Statement and Given. DC covers the Laplace representation in F1, while the crucial choice principle for step 4.1 is HB: F4 provides a separating functional for any fixed nonzero vector. Steps 1.1 through 3.1 quantify over an arbitrary fixed functional, so no simultaneous selection of one functional for every vector is needed. The row must retain HB as well as DC.

The fixed indicator f0 and its translated intervals explicitly define the counterexample, so no witness family is chosen. DC is stated and hence supplies Countable Choice for the Lp, Sobolev, distribution-embedding, and variation-of-constants suppliers. In step 1.2 a single smooth test with prescribed values at 0 and 1 refutes a weak derivative; uniqueness of the mild solution is supplied by F2.

Steps 1.1 and 1.2 identify the same difference quotient with the generator quotient for the explicitly specified vector T(t)x. Existence of its limit is the definition of domain membership, and a limit is unique. DC is a declared assumption for the commutation supplier F3 used in step 2.1; this equivalence itself introduces no selection of derivative values across times or vectors.

Countable Choice is stated for the Lebesgue and Bochner suppliers. The simple functions in step 2.1 are explicit equal-partition samples f(a+k(b-a)/n), so integrability is witnessed by a specified sequence rather than an arbitrary selection from finite covers. The average estimates in steps 4.1 through 7.1 use only one continuity radius for a fixed t and tolerance, with no simultaneous choice of radii.

The Countable Choice hypothesis matches the average-convergence and Bochner-linearity inputs F1 and F2. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 form a uniquely specified primitive and compute its quotients. The constancy argument in step 4.1 uses the mean value inequality F5 rather than choosing a dual functional at every point. No additional HB or family of derivative witnesses is used in this proof.

Countable Choice is declared for the time-integral interfaces. J_t x is a specified orbit integral; step 1.3 takes defining simple approximants within the Bochner framework and uses translation invariance to transfer their errors. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 take the limit of the explicit shifted-average quotient, so no selection of domain representatives is required to put J_t x in D(A).

Here the exponential estimate is assumed with M and omega, so step 1.1 obtains K directly without an additional DC-based uniform boundedness argument. Countable Choice is declared for the Bochner approximants g_n. The partition size for each finite set of orbit curves is its least suitable integer in step 1.1, and step 1.2 needs only one simple approximation for a fixed tolerance; no choices over all forcing values occur.

Countable Choice is stipulated for the Lebesgue time integrals in the Definition. The mild formulation requires an exponential estimate as part of its hypotheses; the concluding note invokes DC only when obtaining that bound automatically. The four solution notions describe functions satisfying specific equations, and do not choose solutions for a family of initial data or assert existence of classical or strong solutions.

The restriction T_Y(t) is canonically defined, and steps 1.2 and 1.3 compare identical quotient vectors in the two inherited norms; no preimages or representatives are selected. Countable Choice is stated for the integral supplier F3 used in step 2.1. Its density witnesses are the specified orbit averages t^{-1}J_t y, with the integral remaining in the closed subspace Y.

Countable Choice is assumed and is expressly inherited from the translation-continuity and distribution-embedding inputs F1 and F6. Steps 1.2 and 1.3 define the averaged translated derivative M_h as an Lp-valued Bochner integral, then identify it by all test pairings. They do not select one measurable representative for every h or every Lp class. The generator derivative is unique as an Lp class.

Countable Choice appears in the Example and Given and covers Lp completeness, dominated convergence, and the injective distribution embedding. In step 5.1 the normalised bumps can be prescribed by translating one fixed nonnegative smooth bump and dividing by its positive Lp norm; this is a deterministic sequence. The proper-domain witness s^{-1-1/p}1_(1,infinity) is explicit, so neither claim needs further choice.

The Lp counterexample assumes Countable Choice through the translation-semigroup input. For every positive t its testing unit vector is explicitly f_t=t^{-1/p}1_(0,t); steps 1.1 through 3.1 compute its norm and shifted difference. Step 4.1 uses the supremum defining operator norm only as a lower bound from that witness, and never chooses a norm-attaining vector from the unit sphere.

Countable Choice is explicit for the Linfinity Banach-space interface. The counterexample uses the single prescribed class 1_(-infinity,0], whose translated difference equals minus an interval indicator of positive measure in step 2.1. Well-definedness and isometry use translation preservation of null sets, so the proof chooses neither representatives of all classes nor a family of failure witnesses.

Only Countable Choice is assumed here: operator-norm continuity supplies the short-time bound directly in F1, avoiding a DC-based local boundedness supplier. Step 1.1 fixes one positive t within that radius, and step 2.1 constructs V inverse by its convergent Neumann series. In step 4.1 x=V inverse y is uniquely specified. The integrated-orbit and Bochner inputs use the declared Countable Choice, with no further selection.
